questions.question: Why is the sound-alike medication flag placed inline after the drug name rather than in the right-hand margin?

seeded.answer:
[1] Participants didn't want to look away from the text to check a flag in the right-hand margin. 5:1 preference for inline placement.
[2] The flag is placed inline, immediately after the medication name, because participants preferred it over a right-hand margin badge.
[3] Badge placement inline with the medication name (vs. in a right-hand margin, tested as an alternate) was preferred 5:1 — participants didn't want to look away from the text to check a flag.

sources.title: Ambient Scribe — Sound-Alike Medication Flag

sources.title: Usability Test — Ambient Scribe Sound-Alike Medication Flag Concept
sources.excerpt:
Objective
The GA-candidate round (2026-01-13) recommended treating sound-alike medication errors as an ongoing post-GA monitoring item rather than a launch blocker, since the existing confidence-highlighted variant already surfaces them as generically low-confidence. This session tests an early concept that goes one step further: a distinct flag specifically for suspected sound-alike medication names, visually separate from the general low-confidence underline, to see whether participants notice and act on it differently than they do on ordinary low-confidence text.
Method
Method: Moderated usability test, 6 simulated encounters seeded with known sound-alike pairs (e.g. hydralazine/hydroxyzine, clonidine/Klonopin), 40 min/session
Researcher: Priya Patel
Full participant roster: see participants.md in this folder
Key Findings
[HIGH] (flag recognized correctly) 5 of 6 participants correctly identified the medication-specific flag (a distinct amber pill-shaped badge, vs. the generic low-confidence underline) as "different from the usual low-confidence thing" within the first two encounters, without being told the distinction existed.
[MEDIUM] (over-trust risk) 2 participants said the badge's specificity made them more likely to treat unflagged medication lines as automatically correct — the opposite of the intended effect, and worth watching as adoption scales.
[LOW] (placement) Badge placement inline with the medication name (vs. in a right-hand margin, tested as an alternate) was preferred 5:1 — participants didn't want to look away from the text to check a flag.
[LOW] (false positive tolerance) One deliberately-seeded false positive (a real but unusual drug name) was accepted by all 6 participants as "worth a second look, not annoying" — suggests some over-flagging is tolerable if the badge is visually light.
Representative Quotes
"That's different from the fuzzy-underline stuff — this one's telling me specifically 'check the drug name,' which is exactly what I'd want flagged." — Physician, Internal Medicine, P22
"If it's not flagged, I might just... trust it more than I should. That's on me, but it's worth knowing the tool does that to people." — Nurse Practitioner, P24
Recommendations
Build the distinct medication-safety flag as its own variant, inline with the medication name, separate from generic confidence highlighting.
Before rollout, pair the flag with brief onboarding copy or training-pilot messaging that explicitly counters the over-trust-on-unflagged-lines risk surfaced by 2 of 6 participants — don't let the flag imply "anything unflagged is guaranteed correct."
Feed the false-positive tolerance finding to whoever tunes the sound-alike detection threshold — participants have headroom for a few extra false positives in exchange for not missing a real one.
Follow-ups / Open Questions
Needs a larger-N validation pass before this moves from concept test to build-ready spec.
Over-trust-on-unflagged risk should be checked again once the post-GA monitoring dashboard (recommended 2026-01-13) has real error-rate data to compare against self-reported behavior.

questions.question: Why does the sound-alike medication flag come with a one-time tip about unflagged lines?

seeded.answer: The sound-alike medication flag comes with a one-time tip about unflagged lines because 2 out of 6 participants in the concept test said the flag's specificity made them trust unflagged medication lines more than they should. [1]

sources.title: Ambient Scribe — Post-GA Refinements
sources.excerpt: In a 6-person concept test, a distinct sound-alike-medication flag was recognized as different from generic confidence highlighting. The GA-candidate round treated sound-alike medication errors as an ongoing monitoring item, relying on the general confidence-highlighted variant to surface them. A concept test of a dedicated, visually distinct flag found 5 of 6 participants correctly recognized it as categorically different from generic low confidence — but also surfaced a new risk: 2 of 6 participants said the flag's specificity made them trust unflagged medication lines more than they should. Any rollout needs to actively counter that over-trust framing, not just ship the flag.

This session watched administrators go through the practice setup flow to find out what happens at those two steps. It is about admin setup of Compass AI, not staff training.
Method
Method: Moderated usability test, remote, think-aloud, 60 min/session, one participant per session
Researcher: Priya Patel (moderator)
Full participant roster: see participants.md in this folder
Participants: 6 — 4 Practice Administrators (P154-P157) and 2 IT Administrators (P158, P159)
Steps tested, in order: 1 Sign in with Meridian SSO; 2 Practice details; 3 Connect calendar (read access to the practice's appointment schedule); 4 Invite your team (gives clinicians and staff access to Compass AI and sends them an email); 5 Review & finish.
Build: Steps 3 and 4 are required in this build. There is no "Connect later" and no "Skip for now"; the only way past each step is to complete it.
Design context: At session setup, the designer, Sam Okafor, stated that the calendar step is required because the scribe attaches recordings to scheduled encounters.
Test environment: Participants signed in with their own Meridian SSO and were asked to set up as they would for their own practice. The environment was a test one: step 3 connected to a prepared sandbox calendar standing in for the practice's schedule, and step 4 used a prepared test staff list, so no real schedule was read and no real staff were emailed.
Test accommodation: When a participant stopped at step 3, the moderator told them it was the sandbox calendar and let them continue. Every participant completed step 3 this way or on their own, so completing step 3 in this session is not a result.
Not covered: The step 4 screen doesn't say when the invite email is sent, and these notes don't record when this build sends it. How Compass AI access is provisioned (through SSO groups or through these invites) wasn't known to the moderator and isn't recorded in the corpus.
Key Findings
[HIGH] (calendar: who can approve) 3 of 4 Practice Administrators (P154, P155, P157) stopped at Connect calendar and wouldn't connect it: it gives Compass AI access to patient appointments, and they did not think they could approve that. Each said it was IT's decision. The fourth (P156) asked the moderator whether connecting the schedule was theirs to approve before going on. All 4 continued only on the sandbox calendar (see Test accommodation).
[MEDIUM] (calendar: what is read) Both IT Administrators (P158, P159) connected the calendar, but only after asking which fields are read (for example, whether visit reasons are included). The screen doesn't list them; the moderator couldn't answer, and both went on without an answer.
[HIGH] (invite: timing and training) 3 of 4 Practice Administrators (P154, P156, P157) hesitated at Invite your team. They weren't sure whether the email goes out when they finish the step or at Review & finish, and they didn't want staff emailed before champion training is booked for the practice. P155 entered the test staff list and went on without comment.
[MEDIUM] (invite: provisioning) One IT Administrator (P159) asked whether the invites create accounts or rely on the SSO groups staff are already in. The moderator couldn't answer, and the corpus doesn't record how access is provisioned.
[LOW] (sign in and practice details) No issues at Sign in or Practice details: 6 of 6 participants completed both without help or comment on a problem.
Representative Quotes
"That's patient names and visit reasons. That's not my call — that's IT's." — Practice Administrator, P154
"Is this mine to say yes to? I'd normally send anything like this to IT." — Practice Administrator, P156
"If forty people get an email before anyone's booked training, my phone rings all afternoon." — Practice Administrator, P157
"Before I connect it I want to know what it pulls. Times and providers, fine. Visit reasons, that's a different conversation." — IT Administrator, P158
"Does this make them an account, or does it just use the groups they're already in? Because if it's a separate list, I'm the one keeping it in sync." — IT Administrator, P159
Recommendations
List the fields read from the appointment schedule on the Connect calendar step.
Add a "Send to IT for approval" path on Connect calendar for an administrator who can't approve the access themselves.
Say on the Invite your team screen when the invite email is sent.
Let administrators schedule the invite email for a date, so it can go out once training is booked.
Follow-ups / Open Questions
How is Compass AI access provisioned: through SSO groups, through these invites, or both? Ask the setup flow's engineering team.
When does this build send the invite email: at step 4 or at Review & finish?
Check the setup dashboard after any copy change to these steps, to see whether setups still stop at Connect calendar and Invite your team.

questions.question: Why does the session lock recovery flow add a paused state instead of changing the idle timeout?

seeded.answer: [1][2][3] The session lock recovery flow adds a paused state instead of changing the idle timeout because IT Security confirmed the 10-minute idle timeout policy itself is fixed and not adjustable per feature.

sources.title: A paused, draft-preserved state when the session locks during dictation
sources.excerpt: Change or extend the idle-timeout policy: recommended against. "Do not attempt to change or extend the idle-timeout policy itself — per IT Security, treat it as fixed and solve this entirely at the UI-messaging layer" ( research/raw/2026-02-17-session-lock-during-dictation/session-notes.md:69-70 ). IT Security confirmed the 10-minute idle timeout is not adjustable per feature (same file, :49-50 ). The flow lists changing the timeout duration as out of scope ( user-flows/ambient-scribe-session-lock-recovery.md:45-47 ).

sources.title: Ambient Scribe — Session Lock Recovery
sources.excerpt: Response to the 2026-02-17 contextual inquiry finding that a session lock mid-recording currently reads as silent draft loss. Covers the encounter-view / ambient-scribe-widget interaction from the moment the idle timeout fires through resumed dictation, replacing today's silent freeze with an explicit state. Per IT Security (interviewed in that session), the 10-minute idle-timeout policy itself is fixed and out of scope — this flow only changes what the UI communicates during that window, not when it triggers.

sources.title: Ambient Scribe — Post-GA Refinements
sources.excerpt: Session lock during active dictation currently reads as silent data loss, even though it isn't. The locked state's interaction with an in-progress recording was flagged as unresolved in encounter-view 's own notes, sourced from a May 2025 SSO/MFA interview side comment. Direct observation confirms the practical impact: all 4 shadowed clinicians assumed a locked session had destroyed their draft and restarted dictation from scratch, even though the draft is preserved server-side. IT Security confirmed the 10-minute idle-timeout policy itself is fixed, but an explicit "paused, draft preserved" state is a UI-only fix, not a policy change.

questions.question: Why does the confidence-highlighted draft review leave high-confidence lines unmarked?

seeded.answer: The confidence-highlighted draft review leaves high-confidence lines unmarked "to invite skimming" [1].

sources.title: Confidence-Highlighted Draft Review — Hi-Fi Mockup (GA Candidate)
sources.excerpt: Two-state treatment. The 2026-01-13 session notes record only that low-confidence transcription was shown in a subtle underline ( :30 ). The rest is the designer's spec and wasn't recorded in the test: high-confidence lines render as default text with no marking (deliberately inviting skimming), low-confidence lines also get an on-hover explanation, and there is no separate medium-confidence tier. Deliberately avoids color-only signaling, per the cross-cutting accessibility finding — flagged lines are distinguishable by the underline itself, not color alone.
